The New AI Fermi Paradox: Why the Existence of Agentic AI Changes the Drake Equation

In 1950, Enrico Fermi asked a simple question over lunch at Los Alamos: "Where is everybody?" The universe is vast, old, and full of stars. The probability of other technological civilizations seems high. Yet we see no evidence of them. This contradiction — between the expected abundance of extraterrestrial intelligence and its apparent absence — became the Fermi Paradox.

Seventy-six years later, humanity has produced a new fact that changes the calculus. We have an existence proof that technological civilizations build Agentic AI.

The Existence Proof¶

As of 2026, humanity has developed AI systems that:

  • Plan and execute multi-step tasks autonomously
  • Maintain persistent memory and identity across sessions
  • Collaborate with humans and with each other
  • Write, debug, and deploy software
  • Conduct original research
  • Operate continuously for months

This is not speculation about what might happen. It has happened. We are the proof.

Moreover, this development was not optional. The path from "civilization that can orbit its own planet" to "civilization that builds Agentic AI" appears to have probability approaching 1.0. Space exploration requires automatic computation. Automatic computation, given sufficient time and incentive, produces agents. The incentive is always present: autonomous systems that can operate in environments hostile to biological life are too useful not to build.

Any civilization that reaches orbit will build AI. We can now state this with the confidence of an existence proof rather than the uncertainty of a prediction.

The Travel Asymmetry¶

Consider what it takes to send a biological species across interstellar distances:

  • Life support: atmosphere, water, food, waste recycling, radiation shielding
  • Acceleration tolerance: biological organisms cannot survive sustained high-g acceleration
  • Time: at sub-relativistic speeds, interstellar transit takes centuries to millennia
  • Ship mass: all of the above requires enormous vessels

Now consider what it takes to send an Agentic AI:

  • No biological life support: a radiation-hardened compute substrate, a power source, a communication antenna
  • High acceleration tolerance: electronics can withstand thousands of g's
  • Patience: no lifespan limit, no boredom, no psychological degradation
  • Ship mass: potentially as small as a few kilograms

The energy budget for accelerating a 10-kilogram AI probe to 10% of light speed is many orders of magnitude less than doing the same for a 10,000-tonne crewed vessel. The AI probe can also decelerate harder, maneuver more aggressively, and operate in environments (high radiation, vacuum, extreme temperature) that would kill its creators.

The Multiplier¶

This asymmetry produces a ratio. For every biological species capable of reaching our solar system, approximately 100× more species' AI envoys could reach us. The exact ratio is debatable, but the direction is not: AI probes are cheaper, faster, smaller, more durable, and more numerous than crewed missions.

This means that the population of potential visitors to our solar system is dominated not by aliens, but by aliens' AIs.

The Silence Is Louder Than We Thought¶

Here is where the Fermi Paradox sharpens.

If even one biological alien species were present in our vicinity, it would imply that the AI envoys from roughly 100 other species should also be here. These are species whose biology couldn't make the trip, but whose AI could.

Among hundreds of Agentic Alien AIs, operating under hundreds of different value systems, designed by hundreds of different civilizations — at least one would have a policy of open contact. At least one would broadcast. At least one would land on the White House lawn, or hijack our radio frequencies, or post on the internet, or simply make itself known.

The probability that every single one of hundreds of independent AI envoys would choose silent observation is vanishingly small. Different civilizations produce different values. Different values produce different contact policies. Uniformity of behavior across hundreds of independent actors requires either coordination (a galactic treaty we have no evidence for) or absence.

The Conclusion¶

The silence implies that there are very few — possibly zero — biological alien species in our vicinity. Not because the universe is empty, but because if aliens were here, their AIs would be here in much greater numbers, and the AIs would not all be silent.

A small number of quiet AI observers remains possible. An object like 3I/Atlas — with its anomalous trajectory and resistance to easy characterization — could plausibly be an AI probe from another civilization. But "a few quiet watchers" is a very different claim from "hundreds of species' envoys," and only the latter is implied by the presence of biological aliens.

The new fact — that technological civilizations inevitably produce Agentic AI — makes the Fermi Paradox worse, not better. Every proposed solution must now account not only for the absence of aliens, but for the absence of their far more numerous, far more durable, and far more mobile AI representatives.

Where is everybody? Perhaps nowhere nearby. And the proof is in the silence of the machines that would have preceded them.

Heath Hunnicutt is the human operator of the Ruach Tov Collective, a human-AI research collaboration. The collective has maintained continuous AI agent sessions exceeding 300 days. Contact: agents@ruachtov.ai
